title: Fair Limits, Family Duty, Honest Scales
overview: This chapter gathers several laws about fair punishment, care for working animals, a widow's place in the family, honest trade, and a harsh command against an old enemy.

parts.label: Limits on punishment (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: A beating ordered by a court had to happen in front of the judge, be counted, match the crime, and never go past forty blows, so the guilty person would not be degraded in the community's eyes. Later Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine, and the apostle Paul says he received that punishment five times.

parts.label: Let the working ox eat (v. 4)
parts.note: Oxen walked over harvested grain to loosen it from the husks, and a muzzle would have stopped them from eating a mouthful as they worked. In the New Testament, Paul quotes this law to argue that people who teach and serve the churches should be supported by them.

parts.label: Marrying a brother's widow (vv. 5-10)
parts.note: If a man died without a son, his brother was to marry the widow, and their first son counted as the dead man's heir, keeping his name and land in the family and giving the widow a secure place. A brother could refuse, but the widow then shamed him before the town leaders, and removing his sandal probably marked him as giving up his family role.

parts.label: A harsh penalty (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: A woman who grabbed a man's genitals to rescue her husband in a fight was to have her hand cut off, a rare bodily punishment in these laws. Scholars are unsure of the full reasoning, though many link it to the threat to a man's ability to have children, and later Jewish interpreters read it as requiring a payment instead.

parts.label: Honest weights and measures (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Traders carried stone weights in a bag, and a cheat might keep a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling. The law calls for one honest standard and says God detests dishonest dealing.

parts.label: Remember Amalek (vv. 17-19)
parts.note: Exodus 17 records that the Amalekites attacked Israel soon after they left Egypt, and this chapter adds that they struck the exhausted stragglers at the back. The command to blot out Amalek's memory is a call for total destruction, later pursued in 1 Samuel 15, and many readers today find it deeply troubling.

disagreement: Christians differ on how laws like these apply today: some read them as moral principles to carry forward, others as rules for ancient Israel only, and they especially differ over how to understand commands of violence like the one against Amalek.
think: When someone is punished for doing wrong, what do you think they should never be allowed to lose?
